challenges:
On the practical side, the main challenge is getting accurate administrative data. In England, mental health admin data has been improving, but there are still more limitations in terms of data quality and completeness compared to physical health administrative data. This has an impact on the quality of the studies we can do. Also, data access can be challenging and can take months.

The other challenge is evaluating all the policies that are being put in place. Everything is happening at the same time, and it is difficult to evaluate and provide scientific evidence on how effective/cost-effective these policies are. In addition, it is not always clear how things started and how they have evolved over time, even when asking the people who want them evaluated or the Government.

challenges:
One of the key challenges I experience in conducting mental health economics research is that economic data collection often competes with many other data collection priorities. Participant burden is a particular concern, so there is constant pressure to collect the minimum amount of economic information while still collecting enough to undertake a meaningful economic evaluation.

This is particularly challenging in dementia research, where relevant resource use and impacts can extend across NHS and social care, informal/unpaid care, voluntary-sector support, and costs to people living with dementia and their families. Deciding what to measure and from which perspective, while keeping data collection proportionate and manageable, can therefore be difficult.
interest: I would really value being part of a group where we can share expertise and experiences across mental health economics studies and work together on some of the methodological challenges we repeatedly encounter. There is considerable scope for greater consistency and shared learning across studies, and I would be keen both to contribute my own experience and to help develop practical approaches that can be used more widely across NIHR research.
assist: I think it could be really helpful to have a forum where we can discuss the challenges we keep encountering across different studies and share how we have approached them. There is a lot of potential to avoid reinventing the wheel, particularly around economic data collection, outcome measures and participant burden, and perhaps to develop some shared approaches or practical guidance that could be used more widely across NIHR-funded research.
access: I think one of the main challenges is that the data are often quite fragmented across different services and datasets, and accessing and linking them can take considerable time. From a health economics perspective, even when data are available, they do not necessarily capture everything we need, particularly social care, informal care and wider impacts on patients and families. This is especially relevant in dementia, where the costs and consequences extend well beyond the healthcare system.
use: Missing data are a recurring challenge, particularly as economic data collection can be quite burdensome and participants may not complete all the measures. Some economic methods can also be challenging for participants; for example, we have found that discrete choice experiments can sometimes be difficult to understand, particularly for people with cognitive impairment or other vulnerabilities, which then has implications for how the data are analysed and interpreted. Another challenge is costing: appropriate and up-to-date unit costs are not always available for all the services people use, particularly for community, social care and voluntary-sector services. There can also be considerable heterogeneity in mental health populations, which makes both the analysis and interpretation of economic outcomes more complex.

challenges: I work mainly in LMICs, where administrative data on mental health is essentially non-existent or not easily accessible. That forces primary data collection through surveys, but self-reported mental health is widely treated by economists as subjective and less valid, so publishing in top journals requires layering on objective measures (actigraphy or wearables for my insomnia work, and biomarkers such as hair, blood or saliva samples elsewhere). Objective data collection at scale is very expensive, and the obvious alternatives don't exist: there is no infrastructure for routinely recorded clinical data, no feasible survey-to-admin linkage, and even if there were, care avoidance means public-facility records would capture a selected sliver of the population. The result is a costly cycle: collect your own data, then spend heavily to validate it.
interest: Having recently moved to a UK institution (a business school to be specific), I'm looking for a community of researchers working on the economics of mental health. It remains a niche field within economics, and most of us sit isolated in departments where nobody else works on these topics. I'd also value a bridge into the NIHR ecosystem, which I'm new to.
assist: Three ways: convening a regular seminar or work-in-progress series where mental health economists can get specialist feedback; working toward shared standards on measurement, particularly on when self-reported scales are acceptable and how to validate them cost-effectively, which would help the whole field defend its data to journals and funders; and funding navigation, especially guidance on NIHR routes for economics-led mental health research, including global health streams for those of us working in LMICs.
access: In the LMIC settings where I work, the challenge is absence rather than access: there is little or no administrative mental health data to request, and no linkage infrastructure connecting surveys to records. Where clinical data exists, governance frameworks for sharing are often undeveloped, making approval processes slow and unpredictable.
use: Measurement dominates everything: reconciling self-reports with objective measures that only partially agree; deciding between continuous scores and clinical cutoffs, which can tell different stories from the same distribution; and handling wearable and biomarker data, which arrives as high-frequency raw output requiring processing choices economics training doesn't cover. Beyond that, attrition in panel studies is rarely random with respect to mental health itself, which complicates the causal designs the field needs.
